title: Welcome to Education Reform's Next 30 Years
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: In the founding post of his Substack, Robert Pondiscio argues that education reform must become a practice-focused movement. He recounts hearing Dan Willingham and realizing that cognitive science validated what he had learned in the South Bronx classroom, despite the folk wisdom and neuromyths he had been taught in training. He criticizes reformers and researchers who treated curriculum, pedagogy and classroom culture as a black box, and says the policy theory of change wrongly assumed teachers were already well trained and only needed incentives. He credits the science-of-reading moment and Tom Bennett's researchED as signs the climate is changing. He closes with three guiding principles: bridge practice, policy and research; keep a supportive but clear-eyed view of ordinary teachers; and accept that education is public business subject to scrutiny.
points: Policy reform fixated on structure and accountability while neglecting instruction, curriculum and classroom management, which teachers know determine outcomes.
Teacher training that passes along neuromyths such as learning styles cost students, and the author argues the anger belongs there.
The science of reading and researchED mark a turn toward evidence and practice that routes around resistant institutions.
The standard for any program or pedagogy is whether the vast majority of ordinary teachers can implement it with reasonable fidelity.
Teachers are public employees with influence over a captive audience, and should expect scrutiny.
quotes: Why had I been left to discover Willingham, E.D. Hirsch, Jr., and others on my own rather than in ed school or in professional development? Where was this wisdom and clarity when I needed it, when it might have benefitted my students who had so little margin for error in their education?

A friend and colleague, also a New York City school teacher, once described his ed school and teacher training in terms that mirrored mine precisely: “a mix of folk wisdom, psycho-jargon, wishful thinking, and out-and-out bullshit.

When one high-profile education blogger asked why I wrote so often about classroom management, I wondered why he didn’t. Every teacher I knew was obsessed with it and understood that nothing good happens amid classroom chaos.

Similarly education researchers are mostly content to treat the classroom as a black box, measuring what goes in and comes out, or as if the salient variable is whether the school is a charter or traditional public school with little or no thought given to the school’s pedagogical model or curriculum.

It is not insulting to observe that a number that large means teaching is a job that must be doable at a satisfactory level by mere mortals, men and women of average sentience and abilities. Classroom saints and superstars are interesting and occasionally inspiring, but they are not proof points: If a program, pedagogy, or policy cannot be implemented with reasonable fidelity by the vast majority of the nation’s teachers, it is not a solution.
